summary: Specifies an EAP mechanism for authentication and session key distribution using the GSM Subscriber Identity Module. It enhances GSM authentication so multiple authentication triplets can be combined for stronger keys. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: EAP-SIM lets a phone card log in to a network the way a mobile phone does, over a protocol that carries logins across the Internet. It makes the old mobile login stronger by using several challenges at once.

questions: how to authenticate with a sim card
how does eap-sim authenticate a sim card
subtitle: Using a mobile phone card to log in over the Internet, with stronger keys and mutual authentication.

tldr.problem: The secret inside a GSM SIM card is short and the old mobile login does not authenticate the network, so it is not safe to use on data networks that need longer keys.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-SIM runs the SIM's own secret algorithms on several random challenges at once and combines the results, and it adds a message authentication code so that both ends prove themselves to the other.
tldr.outcome: The method also adds optional identity privacy, protected result indications and a fast re-authentication procedure, but its security still rests on keeping the card's secret key values secret.

facts.label: GSM triplets used in full authentication

today: RFC 4186 is an Informational memo published in January 2006, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It was written by 3GPP and published for information; the memo records that the EAP working group verified that EAP-SIM is compatible with EAP, but that no other review was done, including validation of the security claims.

sections.title: Why EAP-SIM Exists
sections.content:
This document specifies an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) mechanism for authentication and session key distribution using the GSM Subscriber Identity Module (SIM). GSM is a second generation mobile network standard. Second and third generation mobile networks use different authentication and key agreement mechanisms, and EAP-AKA is the EAP method based on the third generation Authentication and Key Agreement mechanism.

GSM authentication is a challenge and response scheme. The A3 and A8 algorithms that run on the SIM can be given a 128-bit random number, the RAND, as a challenge. The SIM runs operator-specific algorithms that take the RAND and a secret key Ki stored on the SIM as input, and produce a 32-bit response, the SRES, and a 64-bit key, Kc. Kc was originally meant as an encryption key over the air interface, but in this protocol it is used to derive keying material and is not used directly, so the secrecy of Kc is critical to the security of the protocol.

Two weaknesses of GSM authentication are addressed. The lack of mutual authentication is one, and the 64-bit cipher key is not long enough for data networks that want stronger and longer keys. EAP-SIM therefore uses several RAND challenges to produce several Kc keys, which are combined into stronger keying material. The client also sends its own random number, NONCE_MT, so that it contributes to the derivation and can detect replays of earlier requests; the memo calls it the client's challenge to the network. The combined RAND challenges and other messages are extended with a message authentication code, which gives integrity protection and mutual authentication. EAP-SIM also adds optional subscriber identity privacy using pseudonyms, result indications, and a fast re-authentication procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-SIM lets a phone card log in to a network the way a mobile phone does, over a protocol that carries logins across the Internet. It makes the old mobile login stronger by using several challenges at once.

sections.title: The Full Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
The full authentication exchange starts with the authenticator sending an EAP-Request/Identity. The peer's answer carries either the subscriber's International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) or, when identity privacy is in effect, a temporary identity or pseudonym. After that, the peer receives EAP requests of type 18, which is SIM, and sends the matching responses. The packets of type SIM also carry a subtype, and on full authentication the first one is subtype 10, Start.

The EAP-Request/SIM/Start packet carries the list of EAP-SIM versions the server supports in the AT_VERSION_LIST attribute, and may also ask for the subscriber's identity. The peer replies with an EAP-Response/SIM/Start containing AT_NONCE_MT, a random number it chose, and AT_SELECTED_VERSION, the version it picked. The version negotiation is protected because the version list and the selected version go into the key derivation.

The server then obtains n GSM triplets for the subscriber, where n is 2 or 3, from an Authentication Centre on the GSM network; the GSM specifications allow between 1 and 5 triplets at a time. Triplets may be stored for later, but must not be reused, except in some error cases. The server's next request is subtype 11, Challenge, which contains the RAND challenges and a message authentication code, AT_MAC, covering them. The peer runs the GSM algorithm, calculates its own copy of the MAC, and checks that the two match. If they do not, it sends an EAP-Response/SIM/Client-Error and the exchange ends.

Because the RANDs come with a MAC that the peer's NONCE_MT contributes to, the peer can tell that the message is fresh and that the sender holds valid GSM triplets. If all checks pass, the peer answers with an EAP-Response/SIM/Challenge carrying an AT_MAC over its SRES values, the server verifies it, and the server sends EAP-Success. The server may also send the derived keying material to the authenticator; the peer derived the same material, so the authenticator does not forward it.
sections.plainLanguage: The full login has five steps: agree on a protocol version, send a fresh random number, run the card's secret maths on the server's challenges, check that both sides got the same answer, and then derive the session keys.

sections.title: Version Negotiation, Identity And Notifications
sections.content:
EAP-SIM includes version negotiation so the protocol can be extended later. It uses two attributes: AT_VERSION_LIST, which the server always puts in EAP-Request/SIM/Start, and AT_SELECTED_VERSION, which the peer puts in EAP-Response/SIM/Start on full authentication. If the list does not contain a version the peer implements and allows, the peer must answer with EAP-Response/SIM/Client-Error and the error code unsupported version.

Identity management is the other large part of this section. The peer identity can be the permanent identity, such as the IMSI, or a pseudonym, and the server can ask for the permanent identity, for any identity, or for the full authentication identity with the attributes AT_PERMANENT_ID_REQ, AT_ANY_ID_REQ and AT_FULLAUTH_ID_REQ, which are mutually exclusive. Several Start round trips may be needed to arrive at an identity the server accepts. The section also covers attacks against identity privacy, and how the identity is passed to the server.

Notifications carry status and result information. EAP-SIM does not protect the standard EAP notifications, but it defines its own method-specific notifications, which are protected in some cases. The notification code is a 16-bit number whose most significant bit is the Success bit. Codes from 0 to 32767, with that bit clear, mean failure, so the server must send EAP-Failure after the peer's response. Codes from 32768 upwards do not imply failure, and 32768 is reserved as the general code for successful authentication. The second most significant bit is the Phase bit: when it is clear the notification may only be used after a successful Challenge or Re-authentication round, and when it is set it may only be used before one, to report a failure, so the Success bit must then be clear. An exchange may contain at most one notification round.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has a version number so it can grow later, and it lets the client hide its subscriber number behind a pseudonym. Notifications tell the client why a login failed or succeeded, and the top bit of the code says whether it is good or bad news.

sections.title: Fast Re-Authentication
sections.content:
In some environments EAP authentication happens often. Because full authentication uses the SIM's A3/A8 algorithms and needs 2 or 3 fresh triplets from the Authentication Centre, it does not suit frequent use. EAP-SIM therefore has a cheaper fast re-authentication procedure that uses neither the SIM algorithms nor new triplets, and takes fewer round trips. It is optional for both the server and the peer, and either side may fall back to full authentication.

Fast re-authentication is based on the keys derived in the preceding full authentication. The same K_aut and K_encr keys protect the packets, and the original Master Key is used to generate a fresh Master Session Key. The exchange uses an unsigned 16-bit counter in the AT_COUNTER attribute, which limits how many successive re-authentications can happen without a full one, contributes to the keying material, and protects against replays. Both sides keep a copy of the counter and start it at one on full authentication. The peer must check that its own counter value is less than or equal to the one the server sent, and on later re-authentications the counter must be greater than on any previous one. The server also sends an encrypted server random nonce, AT_NONCE_S, and the AT_MAC in the peer's response is computed over it, giving a challenge and response scheme.

Both sides should set an upper limit on how many fast re-authentications happen before a full one is needed, and because the counter is 16 bits the theoretical maximum is reached when it reaches FFFF hexadecimal. To use fast re-authentication, the peer and the server must store the Master Key, the latest counter value and the next fast re-authentication identity, and may either store or re-derive K_aut and K_encr.

The procedure uses its own identity, separate from pseudonyms and the permanent identity, which are for full authentication only. If that identity is lost and the network does not recognise it, the server falls back to full authentication. If the server supports fast re-authentication it may include the skippable AT_NEXT_REAUTH_ID attribute in the encrypted data of the challenge message. That attribute carries a new fast re-authentication identity and doubles as a capability flag saying that the server wants to keep using fast re-authentication. If the server does not send it, the peer must discard its fast re-authentication state and do a full authentication next time.
sections.plainLanguage: When a client connects again soon after, it does not have to run the card's secret maths again. It reuses keys from the previous login, with a counter that stops an attacker replaying old traffic.

sections.title: Key Generation And Message Format
sections.content:
On full authentication a Master Key is derived from the GSM authentication values, the NONCE_MT and other context: MK = SHA1(Identity|n*Kc|NONCE_MT|Version List|Selected Version), where the pipe means concatenation and n*Kc is the n Kc values in the order of the RAND challenges. The identity is the peer identity string without terminating null characters, taken from the last AT_IDENTITY attribute the peer sent, or from the EAP-Response/Identity packet if that attribute was not used. Network byte order is used throughout, and if several Start round trips happen, only the last one contributes.

The Master Key feeds a pseudo-random function that produces separate Transient EAP Keys for protecting EAP-SIM packets, a Master Session Key for link layer security and an Extended Master Session Key for other purposes. EAP-SIM needs two Transient EAP Keys: K_aut for the AT_MAC attribute and K_encr for the AT_ENCR_DATA attribute, and the same pair is used in full authentication and later fast re-authentications. Key derivation follows the random number generation in NIST FIPS Publication 186-2, with 160-bit XKEY and XVAL values. On full authentication the Master Key is the seed, and the 320-bit random numbers that come out are split into K_encr of 128 bits, K_aut of 128 bits, and the Master Session Key and Extended Master Session Key of 64 bytes each. On fast re-authentication the seed becomes XKEY' = SHA1(Identity|counter|NONCE_S|MK), and a new Master Session Key and Extended Master Session Key are produced. The first 32 bytes of the Master Session Key can be used as the Pairwise Master Key for IEEE 802.11i.

On the wire, EAP packets begin with the usual EAP Code, Identifier, Length and Type fields, and in EAP-SIM the Type field is set to 18. The Type-Data starts with an EAP-SIM header of a 1-octet Subtype field and a 2-octet reserved field, followed by attributes in a Type, Length, Value format. The Length field counts in multiples of four bytes and includes the type and length bytes, and the maximum length of an attribute is 1024 bytes. Attributes numbered 0 to 127 are non-skippable, so an unknown one ends the exchange with a client error or a failure notification. Attributes numbered 128 to 255 are skippable and are ignored when not recognised. The order of attributes is insignificant and attributes may be nested inside other attributes. Extensions use skippable attributes so that old implementations still work, but the Start messages are not integrity protected, so they must not be extended in this version of the protocol. Because EAP-SIM does not support fragmentation, extensions should not exceed the EAP MTU of 1020 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides end up with the same keys. The card's answers, the client's random number and the protocol version are mixed into one master key, and that key is stretched into the keys that protect the session and the encryption keys that protect the messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations And Claims
sections.content:
The security discussion is long and careful. The A3 and A8 algorithms that EAP-SIM relies on are specified by each operator rather than fully standardised, and some have been compromised, including COMP-128 version 1, although several revised versions exist and the publicly specified GSM-MILENAGE algorithm is not known to be vulnerable. EAP-SIM gives mutual authentication: the peer believes the network is authentic because the network can compute a correct AT_MAC. But the security rests on the secrecy of the Kc keys, so anyone who learns n, which is 2 or 3, GSM triplets for the subscriber can impersonate a valid network to the peer. Given physical access to the SIM card it is easy to obtain any number of triplets.

On identity, EAP-SIM offers optional protection of the subscriber identity against passive eavesdropping, using pseudonyms delivered by the server. A peer that has not yet done an EAP-SIM exchange usually has no pseudonym, so the permanent identity may have to be sent in the clear, and an active attacker impersonating the network may try to obtain it with the AT_PERMANENT_ID_REQ attribute. The document notes that EAP-SIM does not protect the EAP method negotiation, so method downgrading attacks may be possible, especially when the same identity is used with EAP-SIM and other EAP methods. It does not support ciphersuite negotiation. User data should be integrity protected on physically insecure networks, and when EAP-SIM is used inside a tunnelling protocol, the tunnelling protocol should provide cryptographic binding to stop man-in-the-middle attacks.

The security claims section lists the summary. Authentication mechanism: the GSM SIM mechanism, a challenge and response scheme based on a symmetric 128-bit pre-shared secret, with a peer challenge added for mutual authentication. Ciphersuite negotiation: no. Mutual authentication: yes. Integrity protection: yes. Replay protection: yes. Confidentiality: yes, except for the method-specific success and failure indications. Key derivation: yes. Key strength: 128-bit effective key strength, though if the same credentials are used in GSM/GPRS and in EAP-SIM the strength may be reduced considerably, and an active attack using a false GSM/GPRS base station reduces it to almost zero. Dictionary attack protection: not applicable. Fast reconnect: yes. Session independence: yes. Fragmentation: no. Channel binding: no.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is as strong as the secrets inside the SIM card. Anyone who can copy those secrets can impersonate the network, and the same SIM used on an old GSM network can be attacked there to weaken EAP-SIM.

messages.label: EAP-Response/Identity
messages.note: Carries the permanent identity or a pseudonym.

messages.label: EAP-Request/SIM/Start
messages.note: AT_VERSION_LIST carries the versions the server supports.

messages.label: EAP-Response/SIM/Start
messages.note: Carries AT_NONCE_MT, the peer's own challenge, and the selected version.

messages.label: EAP-Request/SIM/Challenge
messages.note: Carries the RAND challenges and a message authentication code over them.

messages.label: EAP-Response/SIM/Challenge
messages.note: The peer runs the GSM algorithms, checks the code, and answers with a code over its SRES values.

messages.label: EAP-Success
messages.note: The server has verified the code and derived the same keying material.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 1 for an EAP request, 2 for an EAP response.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Matches a response to its request.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole EAP packet.

items.title: Mutual authentication
items.text: Yes. The network proves itself by computing a correct message authentication code.

items.title: Integrity protection
items.text: Yes, through the message authentication code on the exchanges.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Yes, except for the method-specific success and failure indications.

items.title: Fast reconnect
items.text: Yes, through the fast re-authentication procedure.
